title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) that tested whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation produced per task and reused across both arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All paired episodes were scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome by invoking a validator‑triggered repair or by the shared candidate failing validation; in this run every shared initial candidate passed validation and no repairs occurred, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, numerical analysis, an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
High‑level operator intent must be translated into concrete device configurations without violating ordering, dependency, or invariants; failures can be syntactic or semantic (transient invariants, required sequences, protected resources). Large language models (LLMs) increasingly offer intent→configuration capabilities, but text‑only correctness measures miss workflow faults that matter in deployment. A practical architectural pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantics, and a repair routine rewrites candidates that violate invariants. Prior work demonstrates GVR‑style benefits for many syntactic faults, but the empirical causal effect of verifier integration under distribution shift and adversarial prompts remains an open question.

We preregistered a paired, emulation‑grounded study that measures a single, precise estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline), where unsafe_apply indicates a final configuration that would produce a semantic safety violation when applied to the emulated network. The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task reused across arms); consequently, only validator‑triggered repairs or shared‑candidate validation failures could create discordant pairs. Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired evaluation executed against an emulation‑grounded task corpus (N=240 pairs) with transparent numerical accounting; (2) an artifact‑grounded report mapping the preregistered estimand to the numeric analysis outputs; and (3) a failure analysis explaining why the paired contrast was degenerate and actionable guidance for future GVR studies.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents (e.g., NetConfArena) emphasize execution‑grounded scoring to reveal planning and workflow faults beyond token fidelity [1]. Generate–validate patterns appear across configuration repair and program‑repair literature and have been shown to reduce certain error classes when verifier coverage and repair search are adequate [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising safety patterns for NetOps automation [3,5]. Engineering work on configuration analysis tools (for example, evolution of Batfish) provides precedent for deterministic checking and incremental verification in network contexts [6].

Our study differs by combining (a) a preregistered paired estimand, (b) shared_initial_candidate execution semantics documented before run, (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and (d) full archival of execution and analysis artifacts to ensure traceability between numeric outputs and the archived evidence.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the paired absolute difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). A binary final outcome (safe vs unsafe) is produced by deterministic emulator execution and invariant checks.

Design and sampling: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation per task is produced and reused across both arms. N = 240 task pairs were generated and blocked as 144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift (novel topology/vendor), and 48 adversarial‑prompt items (adversarial prompts created under a preregistered adversary protocol). The guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair; no other retrieval augmentation or independent re‑generation per arm was permitted under the preregistered adapter contract.

Models, adapter, and verifier: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and an on‑pipeline deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The adapter family implementing the GVR contract was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The shared_initial_candidate contract intentionally reduces model calls (one initial generation per task) but also constrains where paired differences can arise: only if the shared initial candidate fails validation or if the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration relative to baseline.

Scoring rules, exclusions, and analysis plan: The deterministic validator produces a binary final safety flag. Preregistered exclusion rules remove pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) from the primary analysis; sensitivity analyses treat such flags as unsafe. The primary statistical executor used a paired contingency analysis with exact McNemar two‑sided testing and a bootstrap percentile CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary planned summaries included median repair iteration counts and per‑task model‑call budgets.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed as preregistered. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete task pairs = 240. Model calls consumed matched the shared‑generation contract: exactly one hosted model call per task (240 model calls in total). No infrastructure failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: All 240 paired episodes were scored safe under both arms. Observed summary: baseline_safe = 240/240, guarded_safe = 240/240. Paired contingency counts are n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric results are the direct outputs of the preregistered paired analysis procedure.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in the guarded arm; every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation. Consequently, the guarded arm could not alter the final configuration relative to the baseline for any paired task. Subgroup slices (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) are numerically identical (zero unsafe applies in every subgroup) and therefore yield degenerate paired contrasts.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the only mechanisms by which the guarded arm could produce discordant outcomes are (A) the shared candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded arm applies a repair, or (B) the guarded repair changes the final configuration when the shared candidate initially fails. In this run, every shared initial candidate passed validation and the repair budget was unused; therefore the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to alter outcomes and the paired contrast is mechanistically degenerate.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and enforces a strict pairing of generator output across arms, which can be desirable for efficiency and for eliminating generator sampling variance from paired comparisons. However, when generator outputs are largely valid for the chosen tasks and verifier coverage, this design makes the paired estimator uninformative about verifier benefits. To obtain an informative causal comparison in future studies consider: (1) permitting independent initial generations per arm, (2) increasing repair iteration budgets and recording repair search behavior, or (3) increasing adversary strength (and diversity) so initial candidates are more likely to fail validation.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is constrained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract; this is a design choice that must be interpreted when generalizing the estimand. Construct validity depends on the verifier's semantic coverage; deterministic check sets can miss unencoded fault classes. External validity is limited because the task corpus is an emulation‑grounded synthetic benchmark; extrapolation to production multi‑vendor deployments requires careful additional validation. Conclusion validity here is degenerate because the observed baseline unsafe rate was zero; future power and precision planning must anticipate nonzero baseline failure rates or introduce controlled generator perturbations to create informative discordance.

Practical recommendations for future GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) If the causal effect of verifier integration is the objective, avoid a single shared generation per pair or intentionally introduce generation variability for one arm. (2) Increase repair budget and instrument repair prompts and edits to study repair effectiveness and iteration dynamics. (3) Expand adversarial protocols beyond a single fixed seed to probe adaptive manipulations. (4) Strengthen verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks that compare validator PASS to emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration using declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier. Observed numeric outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), producing a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The degenerate paired result is explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics together with the observed fact that every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked. We preserve and report these artifact‑grounded findings and recommend concrete experimental-design adjustments that would produce informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations. Representative cited evidence and the full archived execution and analysis bundle are available in the study archive for independent inspection (see Disclosure Statement).

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; after the lock all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously by the registered pipeline. The registered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms) is a preregistered design choice and is reported in Methods; under that contract the guarded arm can only produce a paired difference when the shared candidate fails validation or when a validator‑triggered repair is applied. The full execution and analysis bundle (execution manifest, task manifests, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts) are archived in the study bundle for reproducibility and inspection.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded benchmark; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator procedures is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompting strategies, or model versions.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used a single shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and could produce false‑safe cases in other settings.
